title: AMD unveils Threadripper Halo Station, an AI workstation packing 96 cores
content:
AMD unveils Threadripper Halo Station, an AI workstation packing 96 cores and dual liquid-cooled MI350P accelerators — 'the most powerful workstation in the world' can run trillion-parameter models, says AMD
The machine will likely cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.
AMD announced what it calls "the most powerful workstation in the world" at IFA 2026, dubbed the Threadripper Halo Station. The machine includes a Threadripper Pro 9995WX with 96 Zen 5 cores, dual liquid-cooled Instinct MI350P accelerators "with a path to four," 2TB of DDR5, and 288GB of HBM3E with up to 576GB supported. AMD claims the workstation is capable of running trillion-parameter models.
Taking all of the components together, the street price should come out to over $100,000 with just the core components: memory, CPU, and dual GPUs. Configured higher, and with supporting storage, power, and cooling, the workstation could very easily climb over $150,000.
It's essentially a server tray reconfigured into a tower, with an EPYC host replaced with a 96-core Threadripper. AMD didn't share many details about the machine outside of the specs, though it appears to be a system design that AMD's OEM partners will ultimately build and ship. AMD has yet to announce any partners supporting the machine.
The Threadripper Pro 9995WX at the heart of the machine is a 96-core, 192-thread Zen 5 chip that can boost up to 5.4 GHz. It ships with 384 MB of L3 cache and has a TDP of 350W. It's hard to find Threadripper Pro standalone chips in general, but the 9995WX clocks in at around $11,000 to $12,000.
The MI350P accelerators come with 128 CDNA 4 compute units built on TSMC N3. Each accelerator packs 144GB of HBM3E memory, giving the system 288GB of HBM3E. AMD says there's a "path to four," opening up the possibility of two more accelerators bringing 576GB of HBM3E to the system. You'll need plenty of power to feed the GPUs, as each accelerator is rated for up to 600W.
Although AMD says it can support up to four accelerators, the workstation shown off at IFA only has room for two, both of which are liquid-cooled, alongside the Threadripper host. AMD doesn't sell MI350P accelerators on their own in traditional consumer channels, but the estimated price is somewhere around $20,000 per accelerator.
At a system level, the Threadripper Halo Station includes 2TB of DDR5 memory, which is the maximum capacity supported across the eight-channel memory configuration of the Threadripper Pro 9995WX. AMD supports up to DDR5-6400 on the Threadripper, though it made no mention of speed during its IFA presentation. Regardless of speed, 2TB of DDR5 costs about $50,000 right now.

AMD has yet to set a price or release date for the Threadripper Halo Station, though we'll likely hear more about the design from AMD's partners in the near future. An extremely expensive workstation isn't out of the question. The Lenovo ThinkStation P8, for instance, which uses Threadripper Pro CPUs as a host, clocks in at $334,463 right now, maxed out with 2TB of DDR5 and dual Blackwell accelerators.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

report.summary: AMD unveils Threadripper Halo Station, a massive AI workstation with 96 cores and dual MI350P accelerators, targeting trillion-parameter AI models locally.
report.background: The Threadripper Halo Station emerges from the growing demand for on-premises AI workstations that can handle huge models without relying on cloud clusters. It pairs AMD's Threadripper Pro 9995WX—a 96-core Zen 5 workstation chip—with two liquid-cooled Instinct MI350P accelerators, essentially turning a server-class design into a tower. According to AMD, it can run trillion-parameter models, although likely requiring quantization or other memory-saving techniques. The machine also leverages Threadripper Pro's 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes and 8-channel memory, giving it server-level expansion while maintaining higher clock speeds than EPYC. AMD hasn't announced pricing, release dates, or OEM partners yet, but component costs alone could exceed $100,000, and a fully configured system may top $150,000. The move positions AMD's platform as a serious alternative to Nvidia-based workstations like the Lenovo ThinkStation P8.
key_points: The workstation pairs a 96-core, 192-thread Threadripper Pro 9995WX with dual liquid-cooled Instinct MI350P accelerators, providing 2TB of DDR5 and 288GB of HBM3E memory. AMD says there is a potential path to four accelerators and 576GB of HBM3E.

AMD claims this machine can run trillion-parameter models, making it one of the most powerful single-workstation AI systems announced. However, typical large-model inference at that scale usually needs special techniques like quantization or offloading, so real-world performance may depend on software optimization.

It is effectively a re-engineered server tray in a tower form factor: AMD upgraded a high-core EPYC host setup to use a 96-core Threadripper Pro, which still gives 128 PCIe 5.0 lanes and 8 memory channels but with higher 5.4GHz boost clocks than many server chips.

Costs will be extreme: the Threadripper Pro CPU alone sells for about $11,000 to $12,000, each MI350P is estimated around $20,000, and 2TB of DDR5 currently costs roughly $50,000. A fully configured unit could easily climb above $150,000, making this a niche tool rather than a mass-market product.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this signals a push toward putting accelerator-scale capabilities directly on developers' desks, offering a way to test or deploy trillion-parameter models without configuring racks or leasing cloud GPUs. It also sharpens AMD's rivalry with Nvidia in the premium AI workstation segment, especially by combining high CPU core counts with large HBM3E pools. For developers, the Halo Station promises lower-latency, data-resident experimentation with huge models, but only for organizations with deep budgets. For regular users, the technology will likely trickle down over years through smaller chips and cheaper efficiency improvements; immediate influence is limited outside enterprise labs and research institutions.
report.tools: For developers exploring similar AI workloads on AMD hardware, watch ROCm (AMD's GPU compute stack), llama.cpp and vLLM for local inference support, Hugging Face Transformers, and AMD's PyTorch containers. As MI350/CNDA 4 adoption grows, expect broader optimization guides in these open-source projects.
